content: The Greek citron, scientifically referred to as Citrus Medica variety etrog, is primarily associated with its significant role in Jewish rituals during the Feast of Tabernacles. Historically, it was predominantly cultivated on the island of Corfu. However, in modern times, no citron trees remain on the island. Presently, this variety is the most prominent in Israel, where it is highly sought after for religious purposes due to its natural aesthetic appeal and the consistent presence of its style and stigma. In regions such as Crete and Naxos, the Greek citron is distilled into specialized liqueurs. However, for ritualistic purposes, its cultivation is largely confined to Israel. The Greek citron gained prominence within the Ashkenazic Jewish community during the Napoleonic Wars when the importation of the Yanova citron was disrupted due to the ongoing battles. The introduction of this new citron variety raised questions for decades, particularly concerning the lack of clarity about whether the trees were grafted or hybridized. Rabbi Efraim Zalman Margalioth, in his responsa Beis Efraim (Volume 1, Section 56), confirmed during his time that no grafted trees were present on Corfu. This certification, along with the lenient stance of other rabbinic authorities, eventually led to the acceptance of the Greek citron for ritual use. As the Greek citron market expanded, citrons were also imported from mainland Greece, particularly from regions such as Parga, Rapiza, and Agia. However, debates arose regarding whether these plantations adhered to the same standards of kashrut as those on Corfu. Around 1850, Sir Moshe Montefiore initiated efforts to establish citron plantations in Israel to support Jewish settlers struggling with hunger and hardship. Sephardic settlers, who traditionally held a lenient view regarding the Corfu citron, planted seeds in coastal areas of Israel, particularly near Jaffa. Over time, Arab farmers imported cuttings from Greece, which were grafted onto lemon rootstock. The Corfu variety, known locally as Kabbud abu Nunia (the citron with a persistent style), faced challenges adapting to the Palestinian climate, leading to widespread grafting practices. Sephardic rabbis, along with some Ashkenazic authorities, permitted the use of Jaffa citrons after thorough inspections of each fruit. However, the leading Ashkenazic authorities in Jerusalem only approved the Beladdi variety, which was primarily cultivated around Safed, Sh'khem, or the Arab village of Um el-Fahm. Plantations near Tiberias were also deemed acceptable. According to the Hebrew writer Osof Gur in his work Toldos Hoesrog Beretz Yisroel, this variety is characterized by a crisp texture and a slightly sweet inner rind. The pulp, however, is notably high in acidity.
